question: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which entered into force in 2018, regulates the processing of personal data throughout the European Union.

However, in France, disputes of an economic nature appear to be excluded from its scope, even though the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union (judgments C-687/21, C-340/21, C-300/21 and C-634/21) confirms the applicability of the GDPR to such disputes.

This situation is worrying with regard to recovery practices (repeated calls, overcharging, excessive seizures), which particularly affect people in financial difficulties and SMEs. In addition, this exclusion poses a risk to financial stability, as it would allow banks to underestimate their potential losses, thereby distorting the assessment of their risks and capital needs in accordance with Basel III. 1.

Is the Commission aware of cases in some Member States of disputes of an economic nature being excluded from the scope of the GDPR, and can it say whether this practice is compatible with Articles 5, 12, 15 and 24 of the GDPR?
Can it confirm that the GDPR applies to all data processing, including in economic matters?
Does it recognise that there is a danger of the credit risk assessment by financial institutions being distorted, and does it intend to open a dialogue with the French authorities on this matter?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.10.2025) The Commission is not aware of any evidence that some Member States are excluding the disputes of an economic nature from the scope of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)1. The Commission is further not aware of any evidence that the credit risk assessment by financial institutions is being distorted, neither in France nor elsewhere in the EU.

According to its Article 2, the GDPR applies to the processing of personal data wholly or partly by automated means and to the processing other than by automated means of personal data which form part of a filing system or are intended to form part of a filing system. This includes processing in the course of the activities of courts and other judicial authorities (Recital 20).
In accordance with Article 4 of the GDPR, personal data are any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person.
1 Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of

natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation) (Text with EEA relevance), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, pp. 1–88.
